# PART 2 – Respondents in countries {#part-2-respondents-in-countries .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part 2 puts the respondents into the model. We begin with the question of level, what a claim about countries can say about people, then the respondent file that you built from your own downloads after the second day, with the step that turns it into the data of a model, and then three random structures fitted to the same four hundred thousand people, which give nearly the same slope and very different evidence for it, for reasons that the variance components make clear.
:::

## The level of analysis {#the-level-of-analysis .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Contextual**: living through high unemployment changes how everyone in a country frames the EU
- **Compositional**: unemployed people frame the EU differently, so a country with more of them shows a lower average, although nothing has changed for anyone else
- The panel contains no people, so it cannot separate the two readings. An analysis of aggregated survey data "risks committing an ecological fallacy in which aggregate-level relationships are erroneously assumed also to hold for the individual units on which the pre-aggregated data were collected" [@Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling, p. 122]
- A multilevel model keeps both levels in one analysis: the respondents enter it as individuals, and the country-years and the countries as the contexts in which the respondents answered
:::

::: notes
A claim about the effect of a context can be read at two levels. The claim of this case study is about countries, whether the people of a country frame the EU less positively when their national economy does badly. The same words allow a second reading, in which unemployed people frame the EU differently, so that a country with more of them shows a lower average while nothing has changed for anyone else. The first reading is contextual and the second compositional, and the panel of this morning cannot tell them apart, because it contains no people. Fairbrother names the risk: reading an aggregate relationship as if it held for the individuals behind it is the ecological fallacy. The multilevel model is the standard way of keeping both levels in one analysis, and Part 3 uses it to ask how much of the national association composition could explain.
:::

## Levels and evidence {#levels-and-evidence .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-levels-table
# The unemployment slope under three random structures, fitted once on the
# real respondents (companion/_model-outputs/person_multilevel_real.csv)
real_unemp |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    `Random part` = unname(c(two_level = "(1 | cntry)",
                             three_level = "(1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year)",
                             slopes = "(1 + unemp | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year)")[model]),
    Slope = fmt_num(value, 5),
    `Standard error` = fmt_num(se, 5),
    t = fmt_num(statistic, 2),
    `Satterthwaite df` = format(round(df), big.mark = ",")
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Random part", "Slope", "Standard error", "t", "Satterthwaite df")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.75)
```

::: {.small}
- With countries alone, every respondent counts as fresh information about unemployment, although the predictor takes only 270 values: country-year variables "are implicitly taken as individual-level variables, inflating the degrees of freedom and deflating the SEs" [@Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel, p. 25]
- With the country-years declared, the slope barely moves, its standard error grows `r fmt_num(real_unemp$se[real_unemp$model == "three_level"] / real_unemp$se[real_unemp$model == "two_level"], 1)`-fold, and the df fall to the scale of the 270 cells. The random-intercept model of the panel gives `r fmt_num(panel_ri[["Estimate"]], 5)`, t = `r fmt_num(panel_ri[["t value"]], 2)`
:::

::: notes
These are three fits to the same four hundred thousand people. With a random intercept for countries alone, the slope has a t of about minus twenty-five on almost four hundred thousand degrees of freedom, which looks like overwhelming evidence, although every respondent in a country-year shares one unemployment rate, so the model has counted people as if they were countries. Schmidt-Catran and Fairbrother describe exactly this, a variable of the country-year treated as a variable of the individual, with the degrees of freedom inflated and the standard errors deflated. With the country-year level declared as well, the slope barely moves, but its standard error grows about fourfold and the degrees of freedom fall to about two hundred and fifty, the scale of the cells. Once the error structure matches the data, modelling the people and modelling their cell means give much the same answer, which is why the workshop can teach the case study from the panel.
:::

## Random slopes {#random-slopes .smaller}

$$ y_{ict} = \gamma_0 + (\beta + b_c)\, x_{ct} + v_c + r_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict}, \qquad b_c \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2) $$

::: {.small}
- The standard deviation of the country slopes, `r fmt_num(real_sd$value[real_sd$model == "slopes" & real_sd$term == "cntry: unemp"], 5)`, is larger than the size of the average slope, `r fmt_num(real_unemp$value[real_unemp$model == "slopes"], 5)`: the countries do not share one slope
- The df of the average slope fall to about `r round(real_unemp$df[real_unemp$model == "slopes"])`, because the evidence for the average is the 27 countries
- Two analysts of the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] worked at this level. KEVF1 reported t = `r fmt_num(kevf1$statistic, 3)` on about `r round(kevf1$df1)` Satterthwaite df, converted to r = `r fmt_num(kevf1$r, 3)`; PRL47 reported z = `r fmt_num(prl47$statistic, 3)`, with the `r format(prl47$n, big.mark = ",")` respondents standing in for the df, converted to r = `r fmt_num(prl47$r, 4)`
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The same data, the same family of models and the same direction, with converted results `r round(kevf1$r / prl47$r)`-fold apart, almost entirely because of the convention for the degrees of freedom: the unit of analysis and the error structure declared around it are a choice of estimand.
:::

::: notes
A random slope lets each country have its own unemployment slope, drawn from a distribution whose spread the model estimates. The spread turns out to be larger than the average slope itself, so the slopes of some countries are probably positive while the average stays where the earlier fits put it. The degrees of freedom fall once more, to about nineteen, because once each country contributes mainly to its own slope, the evidence for the average is the twenty-seven countries. Two of the five analysts of the robustness study worked at this level, and their converted correlations differ about eightyfold. [advance] With the same data, the same family of models and the same direction, nearly all of the difference comes from the convention for the degrees of freedom, so the error structure that you declare decides which question about 'the effect' you are answering.
:::

## Variance components {#variance-components .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: d3-cosmo-scores
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
# The cosmopolitan score of the respondents, from the aggregate counts saved
# by fit_models.R (companion/_model-outputs/cosmo_dist.csv)
ggplot2::ggplot(cosmo_dist, ggplot2::aes(cosmo, 100 * n_respondents / sum(n_respondents))) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.022, fill = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "cosmopolitan score of a respondent", y = "share of respondents (%)") +
  theme_slide(15)
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
- Standard deviations on the real respondents: `r fmt_num(sd_three$value[sd_three$term == "cntry: (Intercept)"], 4)` between countries, `r fmt_num(sd_three$value[sd_three$term == "cy: (Intercept)"], 4)` between country-years, `r fmt_num(sd_three$value[sd_three$term == "Residual: NA"], 3)` between people. The countries and country-years hold `r fmt_pct(share_groups)` of the variance
- A score is the share of the mentions of a respondent that are cosmopolitan: `r fmt_pct(cosmo_dist$n_respondents[cosmo_dist$cosmo == 0] / sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), 0)` of the respondents score exactly 0 and `r fmt_pct(cosmo_dist$n_respondents[cosmo_dist$cosmo == 1] / sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), 0)` exactly 1
- "[E]stimates of parameters summarizing country effects are likely to be unreliable" with few countries [@BryanJenkins2016MultilevelModellingCountry, p. 3]
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
The variance components say where the variation in framing lies, and almost all of it lies between people, with countries and country-years together holding less than four per cent of the variance. The figure shows why. A respondent who mentions two meanings of the EU, one of them cosmopolitan, scores exactly one half, so the score is bounded and takes only a few values, and about a quarter of all respondents score exactly nought. Within any cell the scatter of such scores is large beside the differences between cells, which is also why so many respondents add so little precision to the slope of a predictor measured on the country-year. Whatever the count of people, the number of countries sets the limit, and with few countries, as the simulations of Bryan and Jenkins show, the estimates of country effects are likely to be unreliable.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – Three random structures {#hands-on-2-three-random-structures .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the IDE workspace**, with `person` from Hands-on 1:

1. Fit the slope with countries alone, then with the country-years declared as well, and read the `df` column of each against the table of levels and evidence:

   ```{.r}
   m_two <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), data = person)
   m_three <- lmerTest::lmer(s_cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year), data = person)
   summary(m_two)
   summary(m_three)
   ```
2. With time to spare, replace `(1 | cntry)` by `(1 + unemp | cntry)` in `m_three`, and read the df once more
:::

::: notes
Fit the two models on your own respondent file, the slope with a random intercept for countries alone and then with the country-years declared as well; on the full file the second fit takes a while. Read the summaries against the table. If every check of your build passed, the numbers should be those of the slide, because your file is the one from which the saved outputs came, and only the name of the scale differs, `s_cosmo` in your formula where my scripts wrote `cosmo`. With time to spare, add the random slope and read the degrees of freedom once more, now at the scale of the countries. If you are following on the slides, read the degrees of freedom in the table from the top row down, and say for each row what the model counts as a piece of evidence.
:::
